question: On the phone, Ela says, “Could you say that again?” What does she want you to do?
choices: Give her a minute to speak.
Repeat the words you just said.
Write your name in a message.
Call her again tomorrow.
note: “Again” asks you to repeat something. “Could you call me back?” asks for another phone call.

question: “Could you speak up a little?” What would help the listener?
choices: A louder voice.
A shorter answer.
An easier example.
A new question.
note: “Speak up” means use a louder voice. “Slow down” is about speed.

picture.alt: A vintage microphone on a stand.

question: “That’s a long address. Could you write it down?” What is the speaker asking for?
choices: The address one more time aloud.
The name of a shorter street.
The way to the nearest bus stop.
The address written on paper.
note: When you write something down, the other person can read it later.

question: At the desk you say, “My surname is White.” The receptionist asks, “How do you spell that?” What do you give her?
choices: Your full home address.
The meaning of your surname.
The letters in your surname.
Your first name and age.
note: To spell a word, say or write its letters. The answer here is “W-H-I-T-E.”

picture.alt: A sealed envelope with a postage stamp.

question: Two people start speaking together on a video call. One says, “Go ahead.” What does she mean?
choices: Please move your chair.
You can speak first.
You can finish the call.
Please say it more loudly.
note: Here “Go ahead” gives the other person a turn to speak.

picture.alt: A laptop with a blank screen.

question: You hear a price over the phone. It sounds like fifteen or fifty lira. You need the exact price.
choices: Sorry, was that fifteen or fifty?
Could you send me the whole price list?
Could you say the price again, please?
Is that the price for one person?
note: A repeat might help. Saying “fifteen or fifty?” tells the speaker which two numbers sound the same to you.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: You can hear your new teacher clearly, but she says the homework instructions very fast. What would help?
choices: Could you speak a little louder, please?
Could you say it one more time, please?
Could I move closer to the board?
Could you say that a little more slowly?
note: A repeat might help. Asking for it “more slowly” also tells the teacher what made it hard to follow.

question: You can read the word “queue” on a sign. You don’t know what it means. What do you ask?
choices: Could you read the word to me, please?
Could you use that word in a sentence?
Sorry, what does “queue” mean here?
Could you show me how to say it?
note: Reading the word aloud helps with its sound. “What does it mean?” asks what the sign is telling you.

picture.alt: An open storybook with a little castle rising from its pages.

question: In a café you point to the small plate under a cup. You want to learn its English name. What do you ask?
choices: Can I have another plate?
What’s this called in English?
Could you tell me what this is for?
Excuse me, may I use this plate?
note: “May I use this?” asks for permission. “What’s this called?” helps you learn a word you can use next time.

question: You can see your classmate on the video call. His lips are moving, but you hear nothing. What do you tell him?
choices: I can see you, but I can’t hear you.
Would you like to call me again later?
Sorry, could you speak louder?
Shall we use text messages instead?
note: A louder voice might help if you hear a little sound. Here you hear nothing, so tell him and he can check his microphone.

picture.alt: A laptop with a blank screen.

question: At the station you hear, “The train to Ankara leaves from platform…” Then a phone rings. Which part do you ask for?
choices: Sorry, can I see the timetable?
Could you say all of that again?
Sorry, is this the right train for Ankara?
Sorry, which platform was that?
note: Repeating everything would take longer. You heard “Ankara”, so “Which platform?” asks for just the missing part.

picture.alt: A travel suitcase with a blank tag.

question: Your teacher says, “Read pages sixteen and seventeen.” You want to check you heard both numbers correctly.
choices: Could you give me the page numbers again?
Could you write the homework on the board?
Pages sixteen and seventeen, right?
Do we read both pages for tomorrow?
note: Repeating the numbers you heard lets the teacher say yes or correct one. Asking for both again is useful if you missed them.

question: A caller asks for Mel. You work with two people called Mel, one in the café and one in the shop. What do you ask?
choices: Could you leave a message for Mel?
Do you mean Mel in the café or Mel in the shop?
Could you call back in a few minutes?
Could you say her name again, please?
note: You heard “Mel” clearly. Asking about the café or the shop helps because both people have the same name.

question: Your friend calls while you’re next to a loud band. You have time to talk and can step outside. What do you say?
choices: Just a moment. I’ll go somewhere quiet.
Could you speak a little louder?
Could we speak another day?
Could you text me instead?
note: Stepping outside removes the noise and lets you talk now. “Could you text me?” would help if you couldn’t leave the noisy room.

picture.alt: A vintage microphone on a stand.

question: You ask what “entrance” means. Your teacher points to the door where people come in. Now you understand. What do you say?
choices: Could you write the word down for me?
Thanks. Could you give me one more example?
Is there another word I could use?
Oh, I see now. Thanks for showing me!
note: An extra example helps if you’re still unsure. “Oh, I see” lets your teacher know the example worked.
